common_name: Pebblebrook Florida Anise (Dwarf Maroon-Flowered Native Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in filtered sun to partial shade; give it several seasons of consistent moisture to fill out its dense, rounded frame.

directions: Pebblebrook is a naturally compact selection of Florida anise that tops out around five feet, making it a better fit than the species for foundation plantings or smaller shade borders. Its two-inch maroon flowers open in mid-spring against dense, glossy evergreen foliage that keeps its shape without regular pruning. Site it out of direct midday sun and keep the root zone evenly moist with a layer of leaf-mold mulch, especially through its first two summers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Grey Ghost Florida Anise (Silver-Variegated Native Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in filtered sun to partial shade; the pewter foliage effect is strongest with some dappled light rather than deep shade.

directions: Grey Ghost was selected by Alabama nurseryman Tommy Dodd for its pewter-grey leaves edged in cream, a variegation pattern noticeably more vigorous and sun-tolerant than his earlier 'Shady Lady' introduction. Pale pink, spidery spring flowers appear against the variegated backdrop, and the shrub often produces a light rebloom later in the season. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil and avoid deep shade, which mutes the foliage contrast; established plants tolerate brief dry spells but color best with steady moisture.

common_name: Scorpio Anise-Shrub (Compact Reblooming Red-Flowered Illicium Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained to occasionally wet, humus-rich soil in dappled sun to partial shade; this compact hybrid, sold under the trade name Scorpio, tolerates more light than either parent species.

directions: Scorpio is an NC State University introduction from the cross of Florida anise and Mexican anise tree, bred for a tidy two-to-three-foot mound instead of the leggy upright form typical of Illicium. Large red-purple flowers open in spring and again in fall, with scattered bloom in between, giving it a much longer floral season than a straight species planting. It handles wetter soils and more direct sun than typical anise shrubs, making it a workable choice for rain gardens or mixed borders rather than shade gardens alone.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Orion Anise-Tree (Compact Reblooming White-Flowered Illicium Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained to occasionally wet, humus-rich soil in dappled sun to partial shade; sold under the trade name Orion, adaptable to clay, loam, and high-organic-matter soils.

directions: Orion is the white-flowered sibling to Scorpio, sharing the same NC State floridanum-by-mexicanum parentage and compact, well-branched habit but reaching a somewhat larger three-to-five-foot frame. Fragrant, strap-petaled ivory-yellow flowers open in spring and again in fall rather than in a single flush, and individual blooms last well over a week. Because it tolerates shadier, damper sites as well as more direct sun than typical Illicium, it works equally well as a woodland-edge specimen or a rain garden shrub.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Plumshine Japanese Anise Tree (Burgundy New-Growth Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in organically rich, evenly moist, acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in filtered sun or partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun; sold under the trade name Plumshine.

directions: Plumshine stands out among Japanese anise selections for foliage that emerges glossy deep burgundy before settling to lustrous green, with fresh burgundy flushes recurring through the growing season. Small ivory, star-shaped flowers with a spicy fragrance open in spring against that colorful new growth. Keep the root zone mulched and consistently moist, apply an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, and shelter young plants from harsh winter exposure until they are well established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
